Training-time defenses (SRPO~\cite{srpo2025}, RobustVLA~\cite{robustvla2025}, DiG-Flow~\cite{digflow2025}, TT-VLA~\cite{liu2026ttvla}) improve robustness but require retraining or reward engineering.

5	\looseness=-1 \paragraph{Inference-time correction.} Among frozen-VLA methods, ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} provides uncertainty quantification but no learned correction; SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} requires task-level RL; VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} uses evolutionary optimization at 2.41\,s per step. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} is the closest concurrent work: it learns a correction head addressing \emph{temporal staleness} within action chunks. Our pipeline targets a complementary problem, namely \emph{initial action quality}, with multi-sample centering, explicit magnitude control, and adaptive per-step compute allocation. Residual policy learning~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual} shares the additive-correction structure; magnitude control is the central challenge, addressed by gating~\cite{jiang2024transic}, RL-bounded clipping~\cite{xiao2026pld}, or decay~\cite{pan2025drc}. Our CRM uses fixed $L_2$ norm clipping with supervised loss, requiring no RL or online rollouts. Conformal prediction~\cite{angelopoulos2023gentle} has been applied to robotics for uncertainty-aware control; our adaptive threshold $\tau$ draws on this calibration philosophy, though the CRM itself conditions only on observation features.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\looseness=-1 Frozen flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can be deployed on new tasks without retraining, but their action quality is bounded by the pretrained policy~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow}. Post-hoc learned correction is an appealing alternative to fine-tuning: a lightweight module trained on task demonstrations can refine actions at inference time with no changes to the VLA weights~\cite{snell2024scaling}. We systematically evaluate this idea and find that it is harmful by default. A Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters) trained on demonstrations and applied unconditionally degrades all four LIBERO suites~\cite{liu2023libero} on SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (0.4B): Long $-$14.8\,pp, Object $-$4.7\,pp, Goal $-$3.7\,pp, and Spatial $-$1.3\,pp. The same pattern holds on $\pi_{0.5}$~\cite{black2025pi05} (3.6B), where unconditional correction degrades all three evaluated suites by up to $-$14.0\,pp on Goal ($3.8{\times}$ the SmolVLA drop). The problem is not the correction module itself, but the assumption that every control step needs correction.

\looseness=-1 Recent work addresses parts of this problem space without confronting the core failure mode. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a correction head on action chunks but applies it unconditionally and targets temporal staleness rather than initial action quality. ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} quantifies uncertainty over frozen VLAs but does not learn a corrective residual. SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} uses reinforcement learning and therefore abandons the weight-frozen constraint. VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} performs evolutionary search at $2.41$\,s per control step, too slow for closed-loop deployment. None analyze when correction helps versus hurts, nor provide a mechanism to suppress correction when the VLA is already confident.

\looseness=-1 Our analysis reveals the root cause: on 80--97\% of control steps, the VLA already produces confident, low-variance actions, and corrections applied to these steps inject noise rather than signal. This observation has a direct consequence: knowing \emph{when not to correct} matters more than the correction's magnitude. To quantify per-step confidence, we construct conformal confidence sets from only $K{=}2$ stochastic action samples drawn in a single batched forward pass. The pairwise $L_2$ distance between these two samples serves as an uncertainty proxy with Spearman $\rho{=}0.9979$ against $K{=}10$ sample variance, at zero extra latency (${\sim}$170\,ms $\approx$ $K{=}1$). A threshold $\tau$ on this distance gates the CRM: when distance falls below $\tau$, the pipeline outputs the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; when it exceeds $\tau$, the CRM applies a bounded residual. This $\tau$-gating mechanism restricts correction to the 3--20\% of steps where the VLA is genuinely uncertain.

\looseness=-1 On SmolVLA across four LIBERO suites, $\tau$-gated correction recovers all degradation from unconditional CRM ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp over CRM always-on). Cross-VLA experiments on $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B, 95--98\% baseline) confirm that the failure pattern persists and amplifies on stronger models: unconditional correction degrades Goal by $-$14.0\,pp. A boundary analysis on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla} (7B, deterministic) shows that 97.3\% of steps produce $L_2 < 0.01$; stochastic sample diversity is therefore a prerequisite for multi-sample confidence estimation. Threshold sensitivity analysis across three suites (Appendix~\ref{sec:tau_sweep}) confirms that success rate is robust to $\tau$ choice, and trigger rate correlates monotonically with effect size across suites.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Systematic analysis of unconditional correction} (Section~\ref{sec:failure_modes}): under a K-matched design ($K{=}2$, same $\varepsilon$ and CRM checkpoint), unconditional correction degrades all four LIBERO suites on SmolVLA ($-$1.3 to $-$14.8\,pp) and all three evaluated suites on $\pi_{0.5}$ ($-$2.0 to $-$14.0\,pp). We identify the 80--97\% of confident steps as the source of harm.
  \item \textbf{Conformal confidence sets with $\tau$-gating} (Section~\ref{sec:method}): $K{=}2$ pairwise $L_2$ distance serves as an uncertainty proxy ($\rho{=}0.9979$ vs.\ $K{=}10$ variance) that gates CRM correction to the 3--20\% of high-uncertainty steps and recovers all degradation ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp).
  \item \textbf{Cross-suite validation} (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}): trigger rate and effect size show monotonic correlation across suites, and $\tau$-sweep analysis confirms gating stability across threshold choices.
  \item \textbf{Cross-VLA analysis} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_vla}): $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B) exhibits amplified degradation under unconditional correction ($3.8{\times}$ SmolVLA drop on Goal). OpenVLA-OFT (7B, deterministic) produces near-identical samples that render multi-sample methods vacuous; stochastic diversity is a prerequisite.
\end{enumerate}

1	We show that learned post-hoc correction of frozen flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models is harmful by default. A lightweight Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters) applied unconditionally degrades task success on all four LIBERO suites---up to $-$14.8\,pp on SmolVLA (0.4B)---because the 80--97\% of control steps where the VLA is already confident receive corrections that act as noise. We propose conformal confidence sets as a detection mechanism: drawing $K{=}2$ stochastic action samples in a single batched forward pass, their pairwise $L_2$ distance yields a per-step uncertainty score ($\rho{=}0.9979$ against ten-sample variance) at zero additional latency. A calibrated threshold $\tau$ on this conformal score gates the CRM, restricting correction to the 3--20\% of high-uncertainty steps. This $\tau$-gating recovers all degradation from unconditional correction ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp), with trigger rates that correlate monotonically with suite difficulty. Cross-VLA analysis on $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B, 95--98\% baselines) confirms the pattern: unconditional correction degrades all evaluated suites, with harm amplified $3.8{\times}$ on stronger models. The key finding is that \emph{knowing when not to correct} matters more than correction strength.

5	\looseness=-1 \paragraph{Inference-time correction.} Among frozen-VLA methods, ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} provides uncertainty quantification but no learned correction; SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} requires task-level RL; VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} uses evolutionary optimization at 2.41\,s per step. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} is the closest concurrent work: it learns a correction head addressing \emph{temporal staleness} within action chunks. Our pipeline targets a complementary problem, namely detecting \emph{when learned correction would hurt}, using conformal confidence sets to gate a bounded correction module. Residual policy learning~\cite{silver2018residual,johannink2019residual} shares the additive-correction structure; magnitude control is the central challenge, addressed by gating~\cite{jiang2024transic}, RL-bounded clipping~\cite{xiao2026pld}, or decay~\cite{pan2025drc}. Our CRM uses fixed $L_2$ norm clipping with supervised loss, requiring no RL or online rollouts. Conformal prediction~\cite{angelopoulos2023gentle} has been applied to robotics for uncertainty-aware control; our adaptive threshold $\tau$ draws on this calibration philosophy, though the CRM itself conditions only on observation features.

7	\looseness=-1 \paragraph{Inference-time compute scaling.} Test-time scaling in LLMs~\cite{snell2024scaling} improves quality via best-of-N selection. RoVer~\cite{dai2025rover} transfers this to VLAs with a reward model; DA-SIP~\cite{chun2025dasip} adapts denoising steps per difficulty. Our analysis shows a different pattern in continuous action spaces: learned correction is universally harmful when applied unconditionally, and the key mechanism is conformal gating---knowing \emph{when not to correct}---rather than scaling sample count (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}).
